This is technically election fraud not voter fraud. Both voter fraud and election fraud fall under the category of electoral fraud, but when discussing this type of fraud I think it's necessary to make the distinction.

  • With Voter Fraud someone is attempting to manipulate votes before they reach the voting ballot. This can include individuals attempting to vote multiple times, or organizations paying individuals for votes.
  • Election fraud occurs at or on the other side of the ballot box. With election fraud, someone behind the scenes is stuffing the ballot box, intentionally miscounting votes, creating confusing ballots, or generally tampering with the record keeping.

This key distinction comes heavily into play when we are discussing voting laws and restrictions. Focusing on voter fraud pushes the discussion towards the voters themselves, and we frequently see this talking point when discussing limitations on who can vote (e.g. Voter ID laws that might make it more difficult for poor people to vote). Talking about election fraud moves the conversation in the direction of how we manage the votes that we're counting. We see this from time to time when it's discovered that someone managed to get a bunch of dead people to vote for them. Unfortunately, I can't think of a good example of when this type of fraud has resulted in a meaningful discussion of election reform.

From what we can tell, voter fraud is minimal and easy to catch. While election fraud can be hidden within the vote counting process. Election fraud does seem to get discovered from time to time, but nothing seems to come of it.

I see a flaw - the printout with your secret randomly generated number. You are trusting the computer system to give you a unique number, when it could be rigged to print out a duplicate number at whatever frequency desired.

Example: 100 people voting total, 60 for Joe and 40 for Sue. Sue has rigged the system to actually tally 15 of Joe's votes for Sue, but print out duplicate numbers for those 15 people that voted for John to make it look like their votes were tallied for Joe. 60 people now have numbers that show they voted for Joe, but the system has tallied 45 votes for Joe and 55 votes for Sue. As long as people are not sharing their voting numbers, it is unlikely one of the people who had their vote changed will find out they have a duplicate voting number.

The only feasible way I see to marginally mitigate this flaw is some kind of flag that shows if a unique voting number has already been verified. If a voter goes and checks their supposedly unique number, only to see that someone else has already checked it and marked it as verified, then you know the system has been tampered with.

However, we now have two problems. The first is that you need to prevent people from marking numbers as verified that are not their own, and the second is that you are now trusting the verification system to not be rigged or compromised.

All in all it is a very interesting idea, but it just goes to show how very complicated this can become, especially when technology is involved.

There's a lot of ways to solve this as well through technology.

There's a balance between wanting to retain anonymity but also retaining verifiability. In other words we want you to be able to verify that you voted a certain way but nobody else to be able to verify that with any sort of readily available information about you. One way to do this is instead of making the numbers entirely random make them formulated in a public way but using a 'secret key'. So for instance they might be generated from your social security number, the id of the voting center you voted at, various other metrics, and finally a magic word/number that only you know. This creates a unique identifier and you can prove that identifier is strictly yours. These sort of algorithms, known as hashes, can have collisions but with smart algorithms the chances can easily be made to be something like 1 in the number of atoms in the universe. You input all the data, do the math (or more like let an open source program do the math for you) and boom - out comes your verified id. Another cool feature of them is that they're 1-way. You can't simple take an id and work your way backwards from it. The only reason we're using the magic word/number is so somebody who happens to know absolutely everything about you still couldn't derive your ID.

This provides a nice balance between anonymity and verifiability. It's effectively impossible for anybody, except you, to link your vote to you and you know that the ID they give is genuine.
